There is a particular hour in the early morning when the world seems undecided.

The streets are empty but not abandoned. Windows hold squares of amber light. Somewhere, a delivery truck sighs at the curb, and a bird rehearses the same three notes as if waiting for an answer. Night has loosened its grip, yet morning has not fully arrived.

I like to imagine that this hour belongs to unfinished things: letters without signatures, books left open on bedside tables, apologies practiced but never spoken. In the half-light, none of them have failed. They are simply waiting.

We often treat uncertainty as a corridor we must hurry through. We want the door, the destination, the clean conclusion. But perhaps uncertainty is not empty space. Perhaps it is the place where possibilities remain alive.

Soon the sun rises. The street acquires names and errands. The windows go dark one by one. Someone turns a key, someone misses a bus, someone decides—without ceremony—to begin again.

The world becomes certain enough to continue.
